\title{Lab 9: Fast Fourier Transform (FFT)}
\titlerunning{Lab 9: FFT Analysis}

\author{Vladyslav Humeniuk}

\institute{}
\maketitle

## Introduction {#sec-intro}

The objective of this laboratory was the empirical verification of the Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) for signal analysis and noise reduction using the GNU Scientific Library (GSL). [cite_start]The Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT) is an essential mathematical tool for decomposing a time-domain signal into its constituent frequency components[cite: 21]. [cite_start]This report details the complete experimental process, including multi-component signal generation, spectral analysis, and the application of frequency-domain filtering to remediate stochastic noise[cite: 21].

## Methodology

[cite_start]The computational procedure was structured into six distinct tasks as defined in the laboratory requirements[cite: 17, 21]:

1.  [cite_start]**Signal Generation**: Synthesis of a 256-element array representing a sum of four cosine functions with varying periods ($k=2, 8, 16, 64$) and amplitudes ($1, 1/5, 1/8, 1/16$)[cite: 17, 21].
2.  [cite_start]**Spectral Analysis**: Extraction of the frequency spectrum using the `gsl_fft_real_radix2_transform` routine[cite: 17, 18, 21].
3.  [cite_start]**Noisy Signal Simulation**: Generation of a cosine wave corrupted by random white noise using a standard pseudo-random number generator[cite: 17, 21].
4.  [cite_start]**Noise Spectrum Analysis**: FFT application to visualize the wide-band frequency distribution of the interference[cite: 17, 21].
5.  [cite_start]**Frequency Filtering**: Implementation of a magnitude-based threshold filter to zero out spectral components with an absolute value below 50[cite: 17, 21].
6.  [cite_start]**Inverse Transform**: Signal reconstruction using the `gsl_fft_halfcomplex_radix2_inverse` function to evaluate filtering efficiency[cite: 17, 18, 21].

## Results

### Signal Decomposition (Tasks 1 & 2)
[cite_start]The initial composite signal demonstrates a complex periodic structure resulting from the superposition of four cosine waves[cite: 17, 21, 23]. Figure \ref{fig-signal} illustrates the high-frequency ripples superimposed on the primary low-frequency oscillation.

[cite_start]![Composite cosine signal generated in the time domain[cite: 17, 21].](1_signal.pdf){#fig-signal width=100% fig-pos='h'}

The frequency spectrum obtained via FFT (Figure \ref{fig-spectrum}) clearly identifies the constituent components. [cite_start]Four distinct peaks are visible at indices corresponding to the input frequencies ($k=2, 8, 16, 64$), with magnitudes of approximately 128.0, 25.6, 16.0, and 8.0, respectively, which align with the theoretical amplitudes[cite: 17, 21, 24].

[cite_start]![Frequency spectrum identifying the four primary signal components[cite: 17, 21].](2_spectrum.pdf){#fig-spectrum width=100% fig-pos='h'}

### Noise Remediation (Tasks 3, 4, & 5)
[cite_start]The introduction of random white noise produced a jagged time-domain function, partially obscuring the underlying wave structure (Figure \ref{fig-noisy-sig})[cite: 17, 21, 25]. [cite_start]In the frequency domain, this interference manifested as a broad noise floor distributed across nearly the entire spectral range (Figure \ref{fig-noisy-spec})[cite: 17, 21, 26].

[cite_start]![Signal corrupted by random white noise[cite: 17, 21].](3_noisy_signal.pdf){#fig-noisy-sig width=100% fig-pos='h'}

[cite_start]![Spectrum of the corrupted signal showing the noise floor[cite: 17, 21].](4_noisy_spectrum.pdf){#fig-noisy-spec width=100% fig-pos='h'}

[cite_start]By applying a magnitude threshold of 50, the noise floor was eliminated, leaving only the primary signal peak intact (Figure \ref{fig-filtered-spec})[cite: 17, 21, 19].

[cite_start]![Filtered spectrum after zeroing components below the threshold of 50[cite: 17, 21].](5_filtered_spectrum.pdf){#fig-filtered-spec width=100% fig-pos='h'}

### Reconstructed Signal (Task 6)
[cite_start]The reconstructed signal after inverse FFT (Figure \ref{fig-inversion}) is significantly smoothed compared to the noisy input[cite: 17, 21, 20]. [cite_start]The periodicity is recovered, and the function is confined to the expected $[-1, 1]$ amplitude range, demonstrating successful noise removal through frequency-domain filtering[cite: 17, 21].

[cite_start]![Smoothed signal reconstructed from the filtered spectrum[cite: 17, 21].](6_inverse_signal.pdf){#fig-inversion width=100% fig-pos='h'}

## Conclusion

The laboratory results confirm that the Fast Fourier Transform is a robust method for analyzing multi-component signals and implementing noise-reduction filters [@gsl_fft_doc]. By utilizing adaptive spectral thresholding, stochastic interference can be effectively isolated from the primary data [@fft_theory]. Reconstructing the filtered signal confirms that frequency-domain manipulation preserves the essential periodic characteristics of the original wave while removing high-frequency disturbances.
